# sql implemented read profiles/v1alpha1

:::info[Reads and catalogue reads implemented on PostgreSQL and MySQL]

Rendered from [`adapters/sql/contracts/reads/v1alpha1/semantics.md`](https://github.com/beyond10x/connectors/blob/main/adapters/sql/contracts/reads/v1alpha1/semantics.md) by `connectors-docs`; the source owns every rule on this page.

:::

This adapter owns the native behavior of its existing local implementation.
Shared wire envelopes and admission remain in
[service v1alpha1](../../../contracts/service.md).
This relocation changes no runtime or selected codec.

SQL: PostgreSQL (and, below, MySQL) schema discovery and parameterized, bounded single-statement reads
through a configured role/database. Database-enforced read-only transactions and
an adapter-owned execution deadline are mandatory. Each transaction installs
statement/lock timeouts as additional server-side guards. Caller-accessible
functions can change those session settings, including between portal executions;
they cannot extend the adapter's deadline. Schema scope is enforced by database grants,
not a string-prefix SQL filter. Preserve column type metadata, NULL, arrays/JSON
and numeric values without silently converting unsupported values into strings.
The first `postgresql-native-text` profile encodes non-NULL cells as PostgreSQL's
lossless text representation alongside each column's native type name; NULL is
JSON null. Numeric precision, arrays, timestamps and JSON are preserved as native
text rather than coerced to JavaScript numbers. Parameters are text or null with
server-side type resolution. This representation is explicit in the descriptor.
Report truncation explicitly; no invented resumable cursor for a fresh SQL query (a
[read profile](#read-profiles)'s keyset cursor follows a column the operator declared, and
is a new read after a value, not a resumed one).
Each request uses a fresh connection and read-only transaction, initialized with
`search_path = public, pg_catalog`; qualify names in other schemas. Session settings
are not a substitute for the configured role's schema and function grants.
No connection pool is claimed in this local profile. A configured CA bundle
replaces public trust roots for SQL; empty bundles are refused.
Do not advertise writes, transactions across requests, or dialect portability.
PostgreSQL SQLSTATE `0A000` (feature not supported) returns `unsupported`, not `unavailable`.
The statement runs as a derived table that closes on its own line; a syntax error (`42601`)
answered to that wrapper, after the statement itself prepared, means the statement is not a
query (`DELETE … RETURNING`, `EXPLAIN`, `SHOW`) and returns `unsupported` (see
[how a statement that is not a read is refused](#read-profiles)).
Source facts: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-set-transaction.html and
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html.
Source access: 2026-09-08.

## Native deadlines and bounds

Within the shared 15 s provider budget (connect &lt;=5 s), execution is at most 10 s
after connection, with up to 2 s reserved for cancellation/cleanup. Slow connection
reduces remaining execution time. Initial statement and lock timeouts are 10 s and
2 s. Native limits are 1,000 rows and 8 KiB query text; callers may request smaller
row limits, but configuration exposes no ceiling overrides.

An independent execution deadline triggers backend-keyed cancellation on failure,
deadline or dropped invocation, using the established endpoint and captured TLS
trust. The supervisor drives cleanup for at most 2 s if the caller disappears,
then closes the connection. Cancellation has no acknowledgement; an unreachable
database, process crash or shutdown may prevent backend termination. Finite local
wait does not guarantee zero query cost or remote termination.

## MySQL engine

A connection whose configuration names `"engine": "mysql"` serves the same
operations, including the catalogue reads below, with the same input bounds, deadlines and
output shape over the MySQL wire protocol; a configuration without `engine` is PostgreSQL,
unchanged, and its effective configuration (and so its revision) carries no `engine` member.
The instance descriptor names the profile `mysql-native-text` for every operation.

Each request uses a fresh session made `READ ONLY` (`SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ
ONLY`) and bounded (`max_execution_time` 10 s, `lock_wait_timeout` and
`innodb_lock_wait_timeout` 2 s), with its `time_zone` set to `+00:00`, before the
caller's statement is prepared. A
statement must return between one and 256 columns, so a statement that returns no
rows is refused as `unsupported` before execution; it then runs as a derived table
with positional column aliases and `LIMIT <limit+1>`, so only one result-returning
statement runs and truncation is reported without draining the result. A statement
that prepares with columns but cannot be a derived table (`SHOW`, `EXPLAIN`), which the
server refuses with error 1064 on the wrapper, is `unsupported`, as on PostgreSQL. A table
write the read-only session refuses (error 1792), including one inside a stored
function, is `forbidden`. The guarantee is that read-only session plus one
result-returning statement; it does not prevent the side effects of a routine the
statement calls. A function the configured user may execute runs with its own
rights: on a live MySQL 8.0.46 a definer-rights function called through
`query.read` ran `SET PERSIST` and `SET GLOBAL`, and the change persisted. The
configured user's grants are therefore the boundary for routines: grant `SELECT`
only, and no `EXECUTE` on a routine with side effects. Parameters are text or
null, bound positionally.

`mysql-native-text` writes every non-NULL cell as a JSON string by its column's
family, never coercing a database value to a JSON number: integers (signed,
unsigned, `YEAR`) as decimal text; `DECIMAL` as the server's exact text; floating
values as the shortest text that reads back as the same value (positional on a
tie, otherwise the exponent form `1e300`, `1e-4`; PostgreSQL writes `1e+300`); `DATE` as
`YYYY-MM-DD`; `DATETIME`, which records no time zone, as the naive local
date-time `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS` with as many fractional digits as the column
declares and no offset; `TIMESTAMP`, an instant, as that instant in UTC in the same
form followed by `Z` (the session time zone is UTC, so the server converts it
before sending it, whatever its own `time_zone`; two distinct instants are never
written alike across a daylight-saving change); `TIME` as `[-]HH:MM:SS[.ffffff]` with
unbounded hours (an elapsed time, not a time of day); binary-charset strings,
`BIT` and geometry as padded standard base64; other strings, `ENUM`, `SET` and
`JSON` as their text. A text cell that is not valid UTF-8 is refused as
`unsupported`, not replaced. NULL is JSON null. Column metadata carries MySQL's
lower-case type name, with ` unsigned` for unsigned integers. The adapter's ESS
model (`adapters/sql/spec/ess`, `connectors_sql.reads`) fixes these rules.

A connection is bound to one database on both engines, and on MySQL a schema is a
database, so `schema.list` on MySQL reads only the connected database: `schema`
may be omitted, which reads it, or name it exactly; any other value is refused as
`invalid_input` before a session is opened or any query sent. It reads
`information_schema.COLUMNS` for that database, returning the PostgreSQL path's
seven columns, and the provenance resource names it; `udt_name` carries MySQL's
`COLUMN_TYPE`. On PostgreSQL `schema` remains required (an input without it is
`invalid_input`) and names a schema inside the connected database.

The connection uses only its configured endpoint (never a server-named Unix
socket), installs no local-file handler, and without `allow_plaintext` requires TLS
before any credential is sent; a configured CA bundle replaces the public roots and
is refused when empty. The adapter's own deadline or a dropped invocation kills the
statement with `KILL QUERY <connection id>` from a second session within the 2 s
cleanup budget, then closes the session; as on PostgreSQL this does not guarantee
remote termination. MySQL errors are classified by number where the SQLSTATE class
is too coarse (access refusals 1044, 1142, 1143, 1227 and 1370 are `forbidden`,
1045 `unauthorized`, 1235 `unsupported`, 3024 `timeout` and 1040/1203 `capacity`,
the last two as the server's answer), and otherwise by SQLSTATE as above. MySQL 8.0
or later is assumed; MariaDB is not claimed.
Source facts: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/set-transaction.html,
https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/server-system-variables.html,
https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/derived-tables.html,
https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/information-schema-columns-table.html,
https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/kill.html and
https://dev.mysql.com/doc/dev/mysql-server/latest/page_protocol_binary_resultset.html.
These MySQL pages were cited, not fetched, when this section was written (2026-10-09);
the wire behavior is checked against a scripted fixture. The ignored live cases in
`adapters/sql/tests/` ran against disposable MySQL 8.0.46 and PostgreSQL 17.11 servers on
2026-10-09; they are not part of the default suite.

## Catalogue reads

Four further reads describe the catalogue on both engines: `database.list`, `table.list`,
`table.describe` and `index.list`. Each is a declared read (`effect: read` in the local
bootstrap) and runs one fixed statement per engine through the `query.read` path: the same
fresh read-only transaction (PostgreSQL) or `READ ONLY` session (MySQL), deadlines, `limit`
of 1 to 1,000 rows, byte limit and explicit `truncated` flag. The caller's schema and table
are bound as text parameters and never written into the statement. Each answer has the
relational result shape of `query.read` under the engine's profile, so every cell is native
text or JSON null; integers are decimal text, and flags are `YES` or `NO` on both engines.
The columns are fixed, in this order:

| operation | input | columns |
|---|---|---|
| `database.list` | `limit` | `database_name` |
| `table.list` | `schema`, `limit` | `table_name`, `table_kind` (`table` or `view`), `row_estimate` |
| `table.describe` | `schema`, `table`, `limit` | `column_name`, `native_type`, `is_nullable`, `column_default`, `ordinal_position`, `primary_key_position`, `foreign_key`, `referenced_schema`, `referenced_table`, `referenced_column` |
| `index.list` | `schema`, optional `table`, `limit` | `index_name`, `table_name`, `column_position`, `column_name`, `is_unique`, `is_primary` |

`schema` follows `schema.list`: on PostgreSQL it is required and names a schema of the
connected database; on MySQL it may be omitted or name the connected database, and any other
value is refused as `invalid_input` before a session is opened. `database.list` takes no
schema: it lists names only and opens no other database. On PostgreSQL it reads
`pg_database`, excluding templates, databases that refuse connections and those the role
lacks `CONNECT` on; on MySQL it reads `information_schema.SCHEMATA`, which shows the databases
the user holds a privilege on (all of them with `SHOW DATABASES`).

`table.list` reports PostgreSQL ordinary and partitioned tables as `table` and views and
materialized views as `view`, and MySQL base tables and views. `row_estimate` is the engine's
own estimate, not a count: `pg_class.reltuples` (null when the table was never analysed) or
`information_schema.TABLES.TABLE_ROWS` (cached statistics, an approximation for InnoDB); it is
null for every view.

`table.describe` answers one row per column in ordinal order. `native_type` is the full type
(`format_type` on PostgreSQL, `COLUMN_TYPE` on MySQL), `column_default` the engine's own text
of the default or null, and `primary_key_position` the column's 1-based place in the primary
key or null. A generated column has no default: on PostgreSQL its generation expression
(`attgenerated`) is not reported as `column_default`, as `information_schema.columns` does
not report it, and MySQL's `COLUMN_DEFAULT` is null for it. A column in a foreign key carries
the constraint name and the referenced schema, table and column paired with it, so a
composite key appears on each of its columns; a column in several foreign keys has one row
per key, ordered by constraint name. A row is one declared key: on PostgreSQL a key into a
partitioned table is reported once, not once more per referenced partition (the internal
clone constraints PostgreSQL keeps on the referencing table, whose parent constraint is on
that same table, are left out), and a partition reports the key it inherits from its
partitioned parent as its own. A table with no row is refused as `not_found`, whether
it does not exist or the configured role or user can see none of its columns: the two are
not told apart.

Foreign keys into what the caller cannot see differ by engine. On PostgreSQL a foreign key is
reported only when the role holds `USAGE` on the referenced schema and some privilege on the
referenced table (or is a member of its owner), as `information_schema` decides, and a column
privilege on every referenced column, so no row names a column that `table.describe` of the
referenced table hides; otherwise each column of the key is still described, without that
key. On MySQL `information_schema.KEY_COLUMN_USAGE` decides: it lists a foreign key of a
table the user can see and names its referenced schema, table and column even when the user
holds no privilege on them, so `table.describe` can name a referenced database that
`database.list` does not list, and a referenced column the user cannot read.

`index.list` answers one row per key column of each index, in index order, for one table or,
without `table`, for every table of the schema; included (non-key) columns are not listed. An
expression key part carries the engine's text of the expression in `column_name`. A table
with no index, and a table that does not exist, are both an empty answer. On PostgreSQL an
index follows column visibility: it is left out when any column it is built on is one
`table.describe` hides (one the role holds no column privilege on and does not own through
the table's owner). That covers a key column, an INCLUDE column and a column used in a key
expression; a column used only in a partial index's predicate counts too, because PostgreSQL
records expression and predicate columns alike (`pg_depend`). A whole-row reference (such
as `(t IS NOT NULL)`, in a key expression or the predicate) is built on every column of the
table, so it counts as every column; PostgreSQL records no dependency for it, and the read
finds it in the stored expression and predicate. PostgreSQL gives an index with no plain key
column a dependency on the whole table (`refobjsubid = 0`), which counts as every column as
well: an index on expressions alone, such as `((pub + 1))`, is listed only to a role that
owns the table or holds a column privilege on every column, even when the expression uses
only visible columns.

MySQL cannot hold a table name that ends in a space, and its metadata collation
(`utf8mb3_bin`) pads, so a lookup of `orders ` would match `orders`. On MySQL,
`table.describe` and `index.list` answer such a name `not_found` before any session is
opened. A name the `utf8mb3` metadata cannot represent (a supplementary character) makes
the server answer error 3988 to the bound lookup; these reads answer it `not_found`, as no
table can carry that name. `query.read` keeps the shared classification, under which 3988
(`HY000`) is `unavailable`. On PostgreSQL both kinds of name are ordinary names and are
looked up as given.

Visibility is the engine's: on PostgreSQL a relation or column is listed when the role owns it
(or is a member of its owner) or holds a privilege on it, as `information_schema` decides; on
MySQL `information_schema` shows only what the user holds a privilege on. The adapter's ESS
model (`connectors_sql.reads.CatalogScope` and the row types `DatabaseRow`, `TableRow`,
`ColumnRow` and `IndexRow`) fixes these rules. The statements are checked on scripted wire
fixtures of both engines. On 2026-10-09 the generated-column, foreign-key, index-visibility
and MySQL name rules were also run against disposable PostgreSQL 17 and MySQL 8.0.46
servers (`adapters/sql/tests/catalogue_adversary.rs` and `catalogue_adversary_2.rs`, ignored by
default).
Source facts: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/catalog-pg-database.html,
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/catalog-pg-class.html,
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/catalog-pg-attribute.html,
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/catalog-pg-constraint.html,
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/catalog-pg-index.html,
https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/information-schema-schemata-table.html,
https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/information-schema-tables-table.html,
https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/information-schema-key-column-usage-table.html and
https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/information-schema-statistics-table.html, cited, not
fetched, on 2026-10-09.

## Read profiles

A connection may declare read profiles in its owner-only native file (`read_profiles`, at
most 32, distinct ids). A read profile is the operator's: one read statement with the
engine's placeholders (`$1`… on PostgreSQL, `?` on MySQL), the names of its parameters in
placeholder order, its output columns in statement order, each with a declared type
(`text`, `integer`, `timestamp` or `phone_number`) and optional masking, the column that
carries the call identifier and the column the keyset cursor follows. The repository holds
only this shape and its validation, which the adapter's ESS model
(`connectors_sql.profiles`, and the profile rules of `connectors_sql.connection.LocalConfiguration`)
fixes; the composition admits a profile exactly when the model does. Profiles are part of
the binding: the effective configuration carries them, so a changed profile is a changed
configuration revision, and a file without profiles (or with an empty list) keeps the
revision it had before profiles existed.

`profile.read` serves them. It is advertised only by a connection that declares a profile,
is a declared read (`effect: read`) and needs no mutation profile. The instance descriptor
publishes each profile's exact input and output as one alternative of the operation's input
and output schemas, so `operations describe` shows the parameters a caller may pass and the
typed columns it gets back. The caller names the profile, gives a value (text or `null`) for
each declared parameter and nothing else, and may pass a cursor and a `limit` of 1 to 1,000.
An unknown profile, an undeclared or missing parameter, or any other member is
`invalid_input`; a cursor the checks below do not admit is `stale_cursor`. Both are refused
before any session is opened. Values are bound as text parameters, never written into a
statement.

A cursor is not signed, so the adapter cannot tell a cursor it issued from one built to look
like it. What it checks is shape, context and type, and a cursor that fails any of them is
`stale_cursor`. Shape: the token is base64url without padding of exactly the object
`{"profile", "context", "after"}` or `{"profile", "context", "after_base64"}`, in the one
form the adapter issues for its value (plain when JSON writes the value without an escape,
otherwise base64url of its UTF-8 bytes), with a value of at most 8,192 bytes. Context:
`profile` names this profile, and `context` is the digest of the instance's revision (which
covers the connection's endpoint, database and user and the full definition of every
profile), the profile's definition and the parameter values, so a cursor issued before any
change to the profile, on another connection or for other values is stale. Type: the
ordering column's declared type admits the value, as it must admit a returned one, so an
`integer` cursor that is not an integer never reaches a cast that would read it as 0. A
cursor that passes all three but was never issued carries a value of the right type for this
read: the ordering column is never masked, so it only moves where a read the caller may make
anyway starts. The longest token the adapter issues (a 64-character id and an 8,192-byte
value that JSON must escape throughout) is 14,795 characters, inside the 16,384 the
published schemas admit; an ordering value longer than 8,192 bytes refuses the page as
`unsupported` rather than issuing a cursor the schemas would refuse.

A page runs the statement through the `query.read` path: the same fresh read-only
transaction (PostgreSQL) or `READ ONLY` session (MySQL), deadlines and byte bounds, and the
same refusals of a statement that is not a read (below) before it runs. A statement that
returns other than its declared number of columns is `unsupported`, also before it runs.
The statement runs inside the derived table with positional aliases, which closes on its
own line on both engines (so a statement ending in a `--` comment cannot reach the
aliases), ordered by one expression `E` of the ordering column and asking for one row past
the limit; a continuation compares the cursor by the same expression:
`… \n) AS result(c0,…) [WHERE E(result.c<k>) > E($<n+1>)] ORDER BY E(result.c<k>) LIMIT <limit+1>`
on PostgreSQL and `… \n) AS result (c0,…) [WHERE E(c<k>) > E(?)] ORDER BY E(c<k>) LIMIT <limit+1>`
on MySQL, where the cursor's value is bound after the statement's own parameters. `E` is
chosen by the declared type and the column's native type when the statement is prepared,
before any row is read (`connectors_sql.profiles.KeysetOrdering`):

| engine | declared type | native column | `E(x)` |
|---|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | `text`, `phone_number` | any | `x::text COLLATE "C"`: the returned text, by its bytes |
| PostgreSQL | `integer` | `int2`, `int4`, `int8` | `x` |
| PostgreSQL | `timestamp` | `timestamp`, `timestamptz` | `x` |
| MySQL | `text`, `phone_number` | a text string (`CHAR`, `VARCHAR`, `TEXT`, `ENUM`, `SET`) | `CAST(CONVERT(x USING utf8mb4) AS BINARY)` |
| MySQL | `integer` | a signed or unsigned integer, `YEAR` | `CAST(x AS DECIMAL(65,0))` |
| MySQL | `timestamp` | `DATETIME`, `TIMESTAMP` | `CAST(x AS DATETIME(6))`, the `Z` of a `TIMESTAMP` cursor dropped (the session is UTC) |

Every other pairing is refused as `unsupported`, naming the profile's column, before the
page is read. Each admitted pairing orders exactly as the cursor compares, and two returned
values are equal under `E` exactly when their texts are equal. That is why the rest are
refused: MySQL writes a binary string, `BIT` and geometry as base64, whose order is not the
order of their bytes; it writes floating, decimal, JSON, date and time values otherwise than
its own text conversion; and an integer or timestamp declared over a text column orders as
text, not as the declared type. ENUM and SET, ordered by their bytes rather than their
index, are consistent. The text expressions also keep a case- or pad-insensitive collation
from tying two distinct values.

A server, or a proxy in front of it, may return fewer rows than any `LIMIT` asks for, so
the adapter never takes a short page for the end. A page that received more than `limit`
rows returns `limit` of them; every page that received a row carries `next_cursor`, after
the last row it returns; only a page that received none is `complete` with a null cursor.
The ordering column must hold distinct values for the rows the statement returns. When a
page received the row past the limit and that row shares the last returned row's ordering
value, the page is refused as `unsupported`, naming the ordering column as not unique:
continuing after that value would drop the row (`connectors_sql.profiles.PageBoundary`). A
shared value inside a page is not a boundary and is served. On PostgreSQL a row past the
limit whose cells exceed the row byte bound cannot be compared, and refuses the page as
`capacity`, as the next page would. The adapter cannot see a row a server cap withheld: when
a server returns fewer rows than asked and a withheld row shares the last returned value,
the next page continues after that value and the withheld row is not returned. Uniqueness
of the ordering column is therefore the operator's obligation; the check above catches it
only where the adapter received the next row.

A statement that is not a read is refused before it runs, the same way on `query.read` and
`profile.read`, and the classes match across the engines. A statement that returns no
columns (an `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE` without `RETURNING`, a `SET`, a `CALL`) is
`unsupported` when it is prepared, on both engines. A statement that prepares with columns
but cannot be a derived table is refused by the server's syntax check of the wrapper, which
the adapter answers `unsupported` too: on PostgreSQL that is `DELETE`, `UPDATE` or `INSERT`
with `RETURNING`, `EXPLAIN` and `SHOW` (SQLSTATE `42601` on the wrapper); on MySQL, which
has no `RETURNING`, `SHOW` and `EXPLAIN` (error 1064 on the wrapper). A PostgreSQL
data-modifying `WITH` is refused by the server as not at the top level (`0A000`), also
`unsupported`. The caller's own statement refused at its own preparation keeps the server's
class (a syntax error in it is `invalid_input`). A write reached at run time through a
function the statement calls is refused by the read-only transaction (PostgreSQL `25006`) or
session (MySQL 1792), and is `forbidden` on both.

Each item carries the declared columns under their declared names, never the database's
own. Every non-null value is a JSON string: `text` the engine's native text; `integer`
decimal digits with an optional `-`; `timestamp` the engine's native text, which starts
`YYYY-MM-DD`, `T` or a space, then `HH:MM:SS`; `phone_number` the number. A value its
declared type does not admit refuses the page as `unsupported`; it is never coerced. A
column is masked when the profile says so, and otherwise exactly when it is a
`phone_number`; a masked value keeps its last four characters and writes `*` for each
earlier one, and a value of four characters or fewer is all `*`. The call identifier and
the ordering column are never masked, are not `phone_number` columns, and are never null:
a null in either refuses the page as `unsupported`. The answer names the profile, its call
identifier and ordering columns and each column's type and masking, so a workflow joins on
the call identifier without a model. A page whose answer would exceed the response limit is
`capacity`; ask for a smaller `limit`.

The scripted wire fixtures of both engines check these rules (`adapters/sql/tests/profiles.rs`,
`profiles_adversary.rs`, `protocol.rs` and `mysql_local.rs`), against a synthetic call table
(`tests/mysql/calls.rs`), including the SQL text of each keyset expression;
`tests/ess_model.rs` holds the executable's admission, masking, pages, page boundaries,
keyset orderings, issued cursors, cursor admission and refusals to the model. No live database has run a read profile yet.
